summary: 1. High-performing Shorts (51%+ stayed, 1,200+ views) open with a direct, counter-intuitive statement in under 12 words rather than setting up context. 2. Low-performing Shorts (24–36% stayed) suffer from wordy academic setups (e.g., 'astronomers are investigating...') or hypothetical scene-setting before making the point. 3. Top titles use high-curiosity pop culture or body-phenomena questions under 7 words (e.g., T. rex, leaking eyes, cutting onions) rather than niche engineering or astronomy topics. 4. Videos under 25 seconds with immediate punchy hooks achieve the highest retention-to-view conversion, whereas long-winded intro hooks drop audience retention under 30% in the first seconds. 5. Rewatchability (AVP > 100%) occurs on deep space/astronomy topics, but initial click/stay rates fail unless the hook is simplified and ultra-short.
winning_hooks: Ultra-short direct assertions under 12 words (e.g., 'Your eyes are leaking right now, and your brain is hiding it.')
Concrete physical visual metaphors in sentence one (e.g., 'pressed down like three small cars stacked on its teeth.')
Immediate myth-busting without setup (e.g., 'The real T. rex probably couldn't run. Not even a jog.')
avoid: Long multi-clause setup sentences over 15 words before reaching the core point (e.g., 'Pluto seemed like our solar system's edge, yet astronomers are...')
Hypothetical roleplay setups (e.g., 'Your car swerves off the highway right toward...')
Niche engineering or obscure industry topics (e.g., guardrail end boxes, salmon color) as primary hook drivers
next_experiment: A/B test a high-AVP topic (space/astronomy) using a 8-word pop-science hook vs. a 20-word background setup hook (e.g., Title: 'Is There a 9th Planet Hidden Past Pluto?' Hook A: 'There is a massive invisible planet hiding behind Pluto.' vs. Hook B: 'For decades astronomers thought Neptune was the end, but new research suggests...')
